*Buddhabhāṣita-romaharṣaṇa-sūtra*, Volume Middle.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Court, the Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial,
the Great Master of Radiant Dharma, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa, the Subject Weijing,
and others, by imperial decree: "Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

I fully know all the paths to the hells and the causes for rebirth therein, as well as the retributions experienced by sentient beings; now, I shall briefly clarify this meaning through a few similes.

Śāriputra! It is as if there were a great mass of fire in the world, equal in height to a person or even exceeding a person’s height; though its flames burn fiercely, they will eventually be extinguished, and the smoke, the flames, and the heat will all completely vanish.

Suppose there is a person who, during the height of summer in the month of scorching heat, when all things are ablaze and the酷暑 (ku-shu) is fearsome, comes from afar, further exhausted and oppressed by hunger and thirst, following the path toward a place where the fire has been extinguished, desiring to find rest.
Beside him was a man with keen vision who saw those suffering intensely from the heat rushing along the path in search of rest.
At that time, the man with keen vision thought to himself:

"That mass of fire is as high as a man, or even exceeds a man's height; when its flames subside, it is not a place of coolness. If this person goes there to sit or lie down, his heat and distress will only increase further, causing him great discomfort and certain extreme suffering."
While he was thinking this, that person went forward and, exactly as he had thought, underwent extreme suffering and distress. Śāriputra,
it is the same for certain types of people who fall into hell!

Whether it be their thoughts or intentions, I know them all; yet because they do not know the practice of the True Path, at the dissolution of the body after death, they fall into an evil destination and are born in hell, where it is extremely unpleasant and they undergo extreme suffering. The Tathāgata, with the pure divine eye that surpasses the human eye, clearly observes this matter.
Śāriputra! For this reason, the Tathāgata is fully able to know the path of the hells and the causes of the hells, as well as all the retributions experienced by sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Those realms of animal existence and the causes for such existence, as well as the retributions experienced by sentient beings therein— I am able to know them all, Śāriputra!"
Suppose there were a heap of foul filth in the world, as high as a man or even exceeding a man's height, filled to the brim with filthy things on all sides.

Suppose there was a person who, during the summer months of the blazing heat when the sun’s glare is fierce and the scorching heat is terrifying, came from afar, further exhausted and oppressed by hunger and thirst, following the path toward that place of foul filth seeking a place to rest.
Beside him was a person with keen vision who saw that one, scorched by heat and in extreme distress, rushing along the path in search of rest.
At that time, the person with keen vision thought to himself:

"That heap of filth is as high as a man, or even exceeds a man's height. If this person goes there, it will not be a place of coolness; instead, his burning affliction will increase further. It is utterly lackluster and not a place to be desired; he will surely undergo extreme suffering."
While he was thinking this, the man went forward and found [the body] either sitting or lying down; it was exactly as he had thought—utterly lacking luster and not at all pleasing to behold.
Śāriputra! There are certain types of persons who fall among the animals; it is just like this.

Whether it be their mind or their intention, I know them all. Because they do not know the practice of the Noble Path, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, they fall into an evil destination and are born among animals—neither radiant nor pleasant, disagreeable, and undergoing extreme suffering. The Tathāgata, with the pure divine eye which surpasses that of humans, clearly observes this matter.
Śāriputra! For this reason, the Tathāgata is fully able to know the animal realm and the causes for rebirth therein, as well as all the retributions experienced by sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Those realms of hungry ghosts and the causes for becoming a hungry ghost, as well as the retributions experienced by sentient beings—all these I am able to know. Śāriputra!"
Suppose there is a tree, as tall as a man or even exceeding a man’s height, which has become withered, decayed, and parched, its branches and leaves having fallen away.

At that time, during the month of midsummer, when the heat is intense and the scorching sun is fearsome, a certain person comes from afar, further exhausted and oppressed by hunger and thirst, following the path to seek rest beneath the withered tree.
Beside him was a person with clear vision who saw that man go beneath a withered tree to seek rest; he thought to himself:
"That man has gone there, but it is not a place of cool refreshment; he will only suffer all the more."
While he was thinking this, the man went forward; whether sitting or lying down, it was exactly as he had thought, and he underwent that suffering. Śāriputra!
There is a class of people who fall among the hungry ghosts (preta), and it is just like this!

Whether it be their hearts or their minds, I know them all; because they do not know the practice of the right path, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall into an evil destination and are born among the hungry ghosts, where they undergo further suffering. The Tathāgata, with the pure divine eye that surpasses the human eye, clearly observes this matter.
Śāriputra! For this reason, the Tathāgata is fully able to know the realm of hungry ghosts and the causes for becoming a hungry ghost, as well as all the retributions experienced by sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
As for that asura path and the causes of asuras, even down to the retributions experienced by sentient beings, I am able to know them all."
Śāriputra! Suppose there is a tree beneath which an anthill has formed, reaching the height of a man or even exceeding it.

Then, during the month of the scorching summer heat, when the sun’s glare is intense and the fierce heat is terrifying, a certain person comes from afar, exhausted and oppressed by hunger and thirst, following the path to reach the shade of that tree in search of rest.
Beside him was a man with keen vision who saw that person going beneath the ant-tree to seek rest, and he thought to himself:
"That person has gone there to a place that is not secure; he will only undergo further suffering."
While he was thinking this, the man went forward; whether sitting or lying down, it was exactly as he had thought, and he underwent that suffering. Śāriputra!
There is a class of persons who fall into the realm of the asuras; it is just like this!

Whether it be their mind or their intention, I know them all. Because they do not know the practice of the right path, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, they fall into the evil realm among the asuras and undergo suffering there. The Tathāgata, with the pure divine eye which surpasses that of humans, clearly observes this matter.
Śāriputra! For this reason, the Tathāgata is fully able to know the realm of asuras and the causes for becoming an asura, up to and including the retributions experienced by sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
All that constitutes the human realm and the causes for rebirth therein, as well as the retributions experienced by sentient beings—all this I am able to know. Śāriputra!"

It is like a tree that is as tall as a man, or even taller than a man, with roots, trunk, and branches all vast and extensive; yet its branches and leaves are not uniform—some parts are sparse and open, while others are dense and thick—and the shade it spreads beneath is likewise entirely differentiated.
Suppose there is a person who, during the height of summer in the month of scorching heat, when all things are blazing and the fierce sun is terrifying,
comes from afar, further exhausted and oppressed by hunger and thirst, following the path toward a tree to seek rest.
Beside him was a man with keen vision who saw that person go beneath a great tree to seek rest and shelter, and he thought to himself:
"That person has gone beneath that great tree; whether sitting or lying down, his experience is a mixture of both suffering and pleasure."
While he was thinking this, the man went forward; whether sitting or lying down, it was exactly as he had thought: he experienced a mixture of suffering and pleasure. Śāriputra!
It is likewise for those sentient beings who are born into the human realm!

Whether it be their hearts or their minds, I know them all; yet because they do not know the path practiced by the Noble Ones, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, they are born into the human realm where they experience a mixture of suffering and pleasure. With the pure divine eye, which surpasses that of humans, the Tathāgata clearly observes this matter.
Śāriputra! For this reason, the Tathāgata is fully able to know the human path and the causes for the human realm, as well as the retributions experienced by sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
All the celestial realms and the causes for rebirth in those destinies, as well as the retributions experienced by sentient beings—all these I am able to know. Śāriputra!"

It is, for example, like a lofty and vast multi-storied pavilion, its walls plastered all around, layered and solidly constructed without any gaps, with its doors, panels, windows, and casements all firmly shut, so that neither wind nor sun can penetrate or shine within.

In the midst of that space, seats were arranged, with red silk brocades used as cushions and rugs, piled up in successive layers to a thickness of sixteen folds, and further covered upon them with white silk.

Suppose there is a person who, during the height of summer in the month of scorching heat, when all things are blazing and the酷暑 (ku-shu) is fearsome, comes from afar, further exhausted and oppressed by hunger and thirst, proceeding along the road, desiring to ascend it in order to find rest.
Beside him was a man with keen vision who saw that person approaching, intending to climb upon it to seek rest and shelter. He thought to himself:

"If this person should ascend this multi-storied pavilion—its windows and doors shaded and closed, its cushions and rugs thick and heavy, most delightful and pleasing to the mind—he will surely experience great joy."
While he was thinking this, the man went forward, ascended the multi-storied pavilion, and whether sitting or lying down, experienced pleasure exactly as he had envisioned.
Śāriputra! It is the same for those who are born in the heavenly realms. Whether it be their mind or their intention, I know them all;

yet because they do not know the path practiced by the Noble Ones, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they are reborn in the happy destinies among the heavens, experiencing delight and happiness. With the pure divine eye, which surpasses that of humans, the Tathāgata clearly observes this matter.
Śāriputra! For this reason,
the Tathāgata is fully able to know the paths of the gods and the causes for rebirth in the celestial realms, as well as all the karmic retributions experienced by sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
All the noble paths to nirvāṇa and the causes of nirvāṇa, as well as the dharmas that constitute the fruit of nirvāṇa realized by sentient beings—I am able to know them all."

Śāriputra! For example, not far from a city in this world, there is a celestial pond, four sides of equal measure, its water pure, limpid, and lovely. All around it, *āmra* trees, *jambū* trees, *pāṇasa* trees, *vaimala* trees, *kubjapīlava* trees, *nāgapuṣpa* trees, and so forth, completely cover all four sides. Those who touch its water find their bodies and limbs greatly benefited.

Suppose there is a person who, during the height of summer in the month of scorching heat, when all things are blazing and the intense heat is fearsome, comes from afar, further exhausted and oppressed by hunger and thirst, constantly following the road and arriving at a pond or pool, desiring to drink its water and bathe his body to wash away the suffering of the heat and exhaustion.
Beside him was a man with keen sight who, seeing that person approaching the pond, thought to himself: "This person has come from afar and is afflicted by exhaustion.

If he goes to that pond, drinks its water, and bathes his body, he will dispel the suffering of heat and fatigue; thereafter, he may go as he pleases into the shade of the trees, sitting or lying down according to his desire, attaining peaceful and secure happiness."
While he was thinking this, that man went forward, and it was exactly as he had thought. Śāriputra,
those people who realize nirvāṇa are also like this!

Whether it be that person’s mind or their mental faculty, I know them all; because they have practiced the path trodden by the Noble Ones, they have cultivated the causes for nirvāṇa and attained the fruit of nirvāṇa. Their outflows are exhausted, and no further outflows increase; their minds are well-liberated and their wisdom is well-liberated, having realized such a Dharma through their own supernormal power.

The Tathāgata, contemplating this matter with discerning vision, saw that those sentient beings, having exhausted their outflows, were liberated; they had realized the Dharma and attained happiness, [knowing]:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence."
Śāriputra! For this reason,
the Tathāgata fully knows the path to nirvāṇa and the dharmas of nirvāṇa, up to and including sentient beings’ realization of the fruit of nirvāṇa.
“Śāriputra! Although that son of a householder knew and saw such matters, because of his lack of faith, he spoke these words:
‘The śramaṇa Gautama!...’”

Since there is not yet even the supreme Dharma among men, how much less could there be the realization of the most excellent noble knowledge and vision? Having entered into debate, he acts as a śrāvaka who proclaims various dharmas; what he seeks and cultivates is realized through his own sophistry and incorrect wisdom. How could the Dharma he teaches lead to liberation or bring an end to suffering?
"Śāriputra! Because of that mental speech and the continuous slander regarding what was seen, they will swiftly fall into hell as if dropping a heavy burden.

Furthermore, just as a śrāvaka bhikṣu who is fully endowed with the training in ethical discipline, concentration, and wisdom attains the realization of the fruit through little exertion without finding it difficult, so too is it for those who fall into the evil destinies!"
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
There is a class of brahmins in the world who practice the rite of fire-worship and consider it to be pure; they say to one another:
'Such-and-such a person, by practicing the rite of fire-worship, has attained purity.'"

"Śāriputra! That practice of fire-worship is utterly impure. It was not that I did not cultivate it in the past; although I practiced it for a long time, it ultimately yielded no benefit, for throughout the vast eons of beginningless time, I did not transcend birth and death."

Yet among the great clans of kṣatriyas, brahmins, and householders, even when they follow their respective practices and seek it for a small portion, they cannot obtain even the superior human dharma; how much less can they attain the supreme realization of noble knowledge and vision?
Why is this? That which they conceive cannot be understood through noble wisdom (*āryaprajñā*), nor can it be awakened to by it.
Since they do not awaken to or understand noble wisdom, how could they be able to find the definitive exit that brings an end to suffering?
Śāriputra! If one awakens to noble wisdom as it truly is, one is able to close the gates of the three realms of existence, exhaust the path of birth and death, and will not be born again hereafter.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
there is a class of brahmins in the world who consider the performance of meritorious gift-offerings to be purification, and they say to one another:
'Such-and-such a person, by performing a meritorious gift-offering, has attained purification.'"

"Śāriputra! That assembly for the distribution of merit is utterly impure. It is not that I did not practice it in the past; although I have gone through its cultivation, it ultimately yields no benefit, because throughout the long eons of beginningless time, one does not transcend birth and death by means of it."
Furthermore, among the kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, elders, and great clans, there are various practices according to their respective views and many kinds of ritual performances, namely:

sacrificing horses to the gods, sacrificing humans to the gods, sacrificing elephants to the gods, and sacrificing sheep to the gods; they establish rites to receive offerings and hold unconfined assemblies (*amogha-pariṣad*).
One performs acts of purification by means of multicolored lotuses;
one performs acts of purification by means of white lotuses;

one performs the ritual for sacrificing to the gods by casting objects into fire, as well as the rituals for Śakra Devendra and the Moon God, and the giving of assemblies such as those involving the production of gold and jewels.

If, through such cultivation, one cannot even attain a small portion of the superior dharmas among human beings, how much less can one attain the supreme realization of noble knowledge and vision? Why is this so?
They are unable to comprehend noble wisdom, nor do they awaken to it.
Because they do not understand or realize noble wisdom, how can they find the path of deliverance to bring an end to suffering?
Śāriputra! If one awakens to noble wisdom as it truly is, one is able to close the gates to the three realms of existence, exhaust the path of birth and death, and will not be born again.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
There is a class of brahmins in the world who, regarding the incantation methods found within their own teachings as pure, say to one another:
'Such-and-such a person has attained purity through these incantation methods.'"

"Śāriputra! That method of incantation is utterly impure; it is not that I have never practiced it in the past, yet despite having undergone such practice, it ultimately yields no benefit, for since beginningless time throughout the vast eons, one does not transcend birth and death through it."

Yet, when kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and great clansmen act according to their own views and seek even a small portion of the supreme human dharma, they are still unable to attain it; how much less so the noble knowledge, vision, and supreme realization.
Why is this? Because they are unable to comprehend noble wisdom and do not awaken to it.
Since they lack comprehension and awakening regarding noble wisdom, how can they find the path of deliverance and reach the ultimate end of suffering?
Śāriputra! If one realizes noble wisdom as it truly is, one will be able to close the gates to the three realms of existence, exhaust the path of birth and death, and not be born again hereafter.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, there is a class of brahmins in this world who, while within saṃsāra and assuming bodies subject to birth and death, consider themselves pure. They say to one another:
'Such-and-such a person, such-and-such a person, while within saṃsāra and assuming bodies subject to birth and death, has attained purity.'"

"Śāriputra! Saṃsāric birth and death are utterly impure. It is not that I have not passed through birth and death in the past; rather, throughout the vast eons since beginningless time, I have been unable to escape them, with the exception of the five Pure Abode Heavens."
Śāriputra! Once born among the Śuddhāvāsa deities, they do not return again to take birth in the human world; rather, they realize nirvāṇa within that very celestial realm.
Śāriputra! For one who has not yet transcended birth and death, even the superior dharmas among humans cannot be attained when sought, let alone the supreme realization of noble knowledge and vision.
Why is this? That which they conceive cannot be understood through noble wisdom, nor can it be awakened to by it.
Because they do not awaken to or understand noble wisdom, how could they find the way out and reach the end of suffering?
Śāriputra! If one awakens to noble wisdom as it truly is, one is able to close the gates to the three realms of existence; having exhausted the path of birth and death, one will not be born again.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
There is a class of brahmins in the world who regard the six destinations as pure, and they say to one another:
'Such-and-such a person, by going to the six destinations, attains purity.'"

"Śāriputra! Those six realms of existence are utterly impure; there is none among them that I have not traversed in the past. Throughout the vast expanse of beginningless time, I have revolved within the cycle of the six realms, with the exception of the five Pure Abodes."

Śāriputra! Once they have been born for one life among the Śuddhāvāsa deities, they no longer return to take birth in the human realm; rather, right there in those heavens, they proceed to realize nirvāṇa.

Śāriputra! Those who have not yet escaped the various realms of existence cannot obtain even a small portion of the supreme human dharmas, let alone the noble knowledge and vision that is the most excellent realization.
Why is this? That which they conceive cannot be understood through noble wisdom, nor can it be awakened to.
Because they do not realize or comprehend noble wisdom, how could they find the way out and reach the end of suffering?

Śāriputra! If one awakens to noble wisdom as it truly is, one is then able to close the gates of the three realms of existence, exhaust the path of birth and death, and will not be born again hereafter.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
There is a class of brahmins in the world who consider their place of birth to be pure, and they say to one another:
'Such-and-such a person, born in such-and-such a place, has attained purity.'"

"Śāriputra! The place where he was born is extremely impure; it is not a place where I have not previously been born in the past. Throughout the vast eons of beginningless time, I have not failed to be born within saṃsāra, with the sole exception of the five Pure Abodes."

Śāriputra! Once they have been born for one life among the Śuddhāvāsa deities, they do not return again to take birth in the human realm; rather, they realize nirvāṇa right there in that celestial destination.

Śāriputra! Those who have not yet transcended birth cannot obtain even a small portion of the supreme human dharmas when they seek them, let alone the most excellent realization of noble knowledge and vision.
Why is this? That which they conceive cannot be understood through noble wisdom, nor can it be awakened to.
Because they do not understand or awaken to noble wisdom, how could they find the way of deliverance or reach the ultimate end of suffering?

Śāriputra! If one awakens to noble wisdom as it truly is, one is then able to close the gates to the three realms of existence, exhaust the path of birth and death, and will not be born again hereafter.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
There is a class of brahmins in the world who, regarding their own seed as pure, say to one another:
'Such-and-such a person, by relying on his own seed, attains purity.'"

"Śāriputra! Those seeds are utterly impure. It is not that I did not rely on seeds for my past births; rather, throughout the vast eons of beginningless time, I have not been born within saṃsāra, with the exception of the five Pure Abode Heavens."
Śāriputra! Once born among the Śuddhāvāsa deities, they do not return again to take birth in the human realm; rather, they realize nirvāṇa within that very celestial destination.
Śāriputra! For one who has not transcended birth and death, even the superior dharmas among humans cannot be attained when sought, let alone the supreme realization of noble knowledge and vision.
Why is this? That which they conceive cannot be understood through noble wisdom, nor can it be awakened to.
Because they do not understand or awaken to noble wisdom, how could they find the way out or reach the end of suffering?
"Śāriputra! If one realizes noble wisdom as it truly is, one can close the gates to the three realms of existence, exhaust the path of birth and death, and will not be born again.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
In the world, there is a class of brahmins who speak thus:
"If one cultivates and fulfills four kinds of dharmas, this constitutes the purity of the holy life."
"Śāriputra! Those who cultivate four dharmas as their holy life (brahmacarya) and thereby attain purity—I am fully able to know them;
among these, I have attained the most supreme state."
What are the four? First, since they are able to practice, I likewise engage in that same supreme practice.
Second, since they are able to cultivate weary detachment, I likewise engage in that same supreme weary detachment.
Third, when they are subjected to intense suffering that afflicts their bodies, I likewise undergo the same supreme intensity of suffering that afflicts my body.
Fourth, when they attain tranquility, I likewise attain the same supreme tranquility.
“Śāriputra! What is meant by practicing in the same manner as those [non-Buddhists]?
It means that if those non-Buddhists constantly keep their hands raised, I likewise do the same;”
Or they do not sit upon beds or mats;
or they constantly remain in a squatting posture;
or they consume food that is foul-smelling and coarse.
Some do not remain fixed in one place but wander about at will;
some shave their hair but leave their beards;
some lie upon beds of thorns;
Some lie upon wooden planks;
some dwell in empty houses;
some remain fixed in one place.
Whether it be bathing three times a day, or even subjecting one's body to various forms of suffering, I shall likewise follow each of their practices.
This constitutes the supreme practice that accords with theirs.
“What is meant by ‘conforming to their supreme renunciation’?
Śāriputra, it means that when those non-Buddhists either discard their robes and go naked, or receive food with their hands raised, I likewise practice accordingly.”
Or one does not accept food from a person with an ugly face;
one does not accept food from a person with a frowning face;
one does not eat food placed between two mortars.
One does not eat food from between two pestles;
one does not eat food from between two staffs;
one does not eat food from between two walls.
One should not accept food from a woman who is pregnant;
one should not accept food from a person handling a frying pan;
and one should not eat from the same vessel as two other people.
If there is a beggar at the doorway, one should not eat there;
if there is a dog at the doorway, one should likewise not eat there;
and if flies or insects are swarming about, one should also not eat there.
One should not accept food from a person who does not speak;
one should not accept food from a person who speaks excessively;
nor should one accept food from a person who says, "Go," and then offers it.
If a person comes and says they will not accept that food;
or if it is food obtained through litigation, he likewise does not accept it;
or he accepts food from only a single household.
Or again, they may eat at two, three, up to seven households;
or they may take one meal and one mouthful, or two, three, up to seven meals and mouthfuls;
or they may eat only once a day.
Or again, every two or three days;
or again, every seven days;
or again, from half a month up to one month, they eat but once.
Among the foods he eats, he does not eat parched grain, nor does he eat boiled rice;
he does not eat small beans;
he does not drink wine made from flowers or fruits.
One shall not drink alcohol made from rice;
one shall not eat meat;
one shall not eat milk, curd, or clarified butter, nor shall one eat honey or products made from honey, nor shall one drink fermented gruel.
They do not eat various kinds of roasted or grilled foods, but sustain themselves by drinking only the water used for washing rice;
or they eat wild rice;
or they eat grasses; or they eat the fruits of thorny trees.
Some eat raw rice; some eat cow dung;
some eat roots, branches, leaves, and fruits of trees.
Or again, he would go specifically into the wilderness to gather various kinds of roots, stalks, branches, leaves, seeds,
and so forth for food. Śāriputra,
as he practiced in such a manner, I also followed his practice.
This is my cultivation of the supreme revulsion.
From the *Buddhabhāṣita-loma-harṣaṇa-sūtra*, middle fascicle;
the *Buddhabhāṣita-loma-harṣaṇa-sūtra*, lower fascicle.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Court, the Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial,
the Great Master of Radiant Dharma, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa, the Subject Weijing,
and others, by Imperial Decree: “Furthermore, Śāriputra!
How is it that he undergoes the same supreme, agonizing affliction of the body?
It means that my own limbs are covered with dust and dirt; at first it is slight, then it gradually increases, and finally it accumulates.
It is like the branches and leaves of the *dinduka* tree: the accumulated dust begins as something minute, gradually increases, and finally accumulates into a great mass.
My own body is likewise! Śāriputra,
although I am covered and defiled by layers of dust and grime, I have never, day or night, entertained such thoughts as these:
"Alas, why is this! This body of mine is now a composite of dust and impurities; who shall be there to sweep these away for me? Śāriputra!
This is what it means to share in that supreme, most intense suffering that oppresses the body.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
how does one share in that supreme tranquility?

That is to say, dwelling, sitting, or lying down in a wilderness or a secluded place, far removed from all clamor and bustle, having cast aside all necessary articles of use, one dwells alone in quietude, abiding as is appropriate.
Śāriputra! At that time,
I likewise conformed to their conduct, whether as a cowherd or as a cattle-keeper.
Some were woodcutters;
some were gardeners; some were travelers on the road.
Having seen these people, I immediately fled to an extremely secluded place so that they would not see me again.
It was like a wild deer that, upon seeing such people as herdsmen, flees to a deep and hidden place to avoid them from afar, out of fear of being seen by them.
My dwelling in the wilderness, far removed from clamor and bustle, is likewise so!
This is precisely what constitutes the supreme tranquility practiced by him.
"Śāriputra! [he said].

Even though one practices in this way, if one cannot obtain even a small portion of the supreme human dharmas by seeking them, how much less can one attain the most excellent realization of noble knowledge and vision? Why is this?
They are unable to comprehend noble wisdom, nor do they awaken to it.
Because they do not understand noble wisdom, how can they find the way of deliverance and reach the end of suffering?
Śāriputra! If one awakens to noble wisdom as it truly is, one can then close the gates to the three realms of existence, exhaust the path of birth and death, and will not be born again hereafter.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, there is a class of brahmins in the world who speak as follows:

'On the eighth night of the first month of winter, when the snow is falling, I shall go to a desolate and remote wilderness or near the side of a river; with my body naked, I shall lie down face-down in the deep snow and remain there throughout the night.'"
"Such practices as these are reckoned as pure.

Śāriputra, I knew this matter and likewise engaged in those practices; thus, on the eighth night of the first month of winter, when the snow was falling, in a desolate wilderness or near the banks of a river, I lay down naked in the deep snow, remaining there through the entire night.

Śāriputra! Although one practices in this way, one cannot even obtain a small portion of the supreme human dharmas when seeking them, let alone the most excellent realization of noble knowledge and vision.
Why is this? Because they are unable to comprehend noble wisdom and do not awaken to it.
Since they do not understand or realize noble wisdom, how can they find the path of deliverance and reach the end of suffering?

Śāriputra! If one awakens to noble wisdom as it truly is, one is then able to close the gates to the three realms of existence, exhaust the path of birth and death, and will not be born again hereafter.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, there is a class of brahmins in the world who speak thus:
'On the eighth night of the first month of winter, when the snow is falling, I go to deep water that reaches above my neck and remain within it throughout the night. "
"Such conduct as this is reckoned as pure. Śāriputra, knowing this matter, I likewise practiced that way;
thus, on the eighth night of the first month of winter, when the snow was falling, I went to deep water that reached above my neck and remained within it throughout the night.

Śāriputra! Although one practices in this way, one cannot even obtain a small portion of the supreme human dharmas when seeking them, let alone the most excellent realization of noble knowledge and vision.
To speak at length, up until: having exhausted the path of birth and death, one will not be born again.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Among the world, there is a class of brahmins who speak as follows:
"In the midst of summer, during the month of scorching heat, at the time when the sun is at its zenith, I shall stand upon sand that has accumulated to a depth exceeding the knee."
At that time, I stood naked with one foot raised; as the sun shone upon me, I turned in accordance with its movement.
Such was my practice, which I reckoned to be pure.

"Śāriputra! I know this matter and have likewise practiced it. Thus, during the months of the intense summer heat, when the scorching sun is most fearsome and at its zenith, I would stand upon deep sand that rose above my knees, my body exposed, standing on one foot while being scorched by the sun, turning as the sun moved."

Śāriputra! At that time, when all the people—whether men or women—learned of this matter, they all rushed there in great crowds, jostling one another in their eagerness to behold it. Amidst the public discussion, my own mind remained naturally composed; I attained a state of joy, felt no mental distress, and gave rise to no sense of weariness.

Śāriputra! Although one practices in this way, one cannot even attain a small portion of the supreme human dharmas when seeking them, let alone the most excellent realization of noble knowledge and vision.
To speak at length, up until the exhaustion of the path of birth and death, such that one is never born again.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
there is a class of brahmins in the world who speak as follows:
"I sought this food through hardship; it was difficult to obtain, and I consider it pure.
Śāriputra, I knew this matter and likewise practiced in that same way.
What is the food obtained through difficult seeking?

It means that I go specifically into the wilderness to where herds of cattle gather, and there I beg for the milk of a calf; whatever I obtain, I use as my food—this is what is meant by food obtained through difficult seeking.

Śāriputra! Although one practices in this way, if one cannot even obtain a small portion of the supreme human dharmas by seeking them, how much less can one attain the most excellent realization of noble knowledge and vision?
To speak at length, it continues until they have exhausted the path of birth and death and shall not be born again.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
there is a class of brahmins in the world who eat only barley, considering this to be pure, and speak as follows:"
"If one eats only barley and practices in this manner, one will attain purity.
Having taken the barley, he would either grind it into powder or soak it in water.
Or they may consume various kinds of medicinal preparations for the sake of nourishment. Śāriputra,
I am aware of this matter, and I likewise practice in that same way.
"What was my practice of taking barley as food?
Śāriputra, I took only a single grain to eat, never adding a second."

Later, at another time, because of eating barley, my limbs became heavy and fleshy, or perhaps even lustrous; yet I did not give rise to the thought that I should exceed the proper measure by taking more barley to eat, for I would take only a single grain and never add a second.
"Śāriputra! Because I subsisted on a single grain of barley, I became so extremely emaciated that my upper and lower body were like those of the kālaka bird and the asata bird."
Furthermore, his feet and calves were withered and thin, appearing loathsome to behold; his feet were no different from those of a camel or a sheep.
Moreover, the bones of his neck and back were exposed, appearing like a pile of stones—some sunken, some protruding—and uneven in height.

They were like an empty, secluded grass hut in an open field, transparent on both sides, with its wooden supports widely spaced and the interior wide open, such that one could see through it from either side.
The joints of my ribs are exposed and sparse, with wide gaps between them that allow one side to see the other.

It is like water exposed to the scorching heat of the sun during the summer months; when someone looks down into it at dusk, the stars appear faintly reflected within, as if they were extremely deep and far away.
My two eyes have become so extremely sunken that they seem as if they perceive something; it is just like this!

Furthermore, it is like a bitter gourd that is green and unripe; when people cut it from its vine, its branches and leaves wither immediately, gradually becoming parched and weak until finally they dry and shrivel together.
My own body, from head to foot, is likewise!
It first becomes withered, then gradually grows weak, and finally becomes so emaciated that only skin and bone remain joined together.

"Śāriputra! At first, I forced my body to maintain its composure, leaning against thorns for support; yet when my strength failed me, I wished to rise but sat back down again. My limbs and joints went limp, my head and neck hung low, and I was so debilitated that I could not speak, like a dumb sheep."

Although I was thus, I remained steadfast; I withdrew my mind within and exerted my body without, skillfully regulating my breath. Yet, as soon as I attempted to raise my body, it was once again smeared and defiled by dust. Because of the accumulation of this dust and filth, the hairs on my body were completely worn away and fell off.
"Śāriputra! At that time, all the men and women from the surrounding cities, towns, and villages rushed forth, vying with one another to behold [the sight], and all spoke these words: 'Alas, alas!'"
"Śramaṇa Gautama!
Your body is emaciated and has become dark blue-black. Your former appearance was exquisite, upright, and dignified, and it also possessed majestic radiance; why has that now vanished?"
“With such bitter and arduous cultivation, yet his appearance remains like this! Śāriputra,

although one practices in this way, if one cannot even attain a small portion of the supreme dharmas among human beings, how much less can one attain the most excellent realization of noble knowledge and vision?
To speak at length, up until the exhaustion of the path of birth and death, one shall not be born again.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
There is a class of brahmins in the world who eat only rice, considering it pure, and they speak thus: [text continues]"
"If one eats only rice and practices in this manner, one will attain purity.
Having taken the rice, he either crushed it into powder or strained out its water.
Or they may consume various kinds of medicinal preparations for the sake of nourishment. Śāriputra,
I know this matter, and I likewise practice in that same way.
"What is this 'taking rice as food' that you speak of? Śāriputra!
I take only a single grain to eat; I do not add a second."

Later, at another time, because of eating rice, my limbs became plump and heavy, or perhaps even lustrous; yet I did not give rise to the thought of exceeding that measure by taking more rice to eat, but took only a single grain, never adding a second. Śāriputra!
"I shall practice asceticism in this manner.
At that time, there were people who came and spoke these words:
"In former days, your appearance was exquisite, virtuous, and dignified, and you possessed a majestic radiance; why has it now vanished?"
"Though he has undergone such rigorous and arduous training, his physical appearance remains like this!

Śāriputra, although one practices in this way, if even a small portion of the supreme dharmas among humans cannot be attained, how much less so the noble knowledge, vision, and the most excellent realization?
To speak at length, up until the exhaustion of the path of birth and death, one shall not be born again.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, there is a class of brahmins in the world who eat only sesame seeds, considering this to be pure, and they speak thus: [text continues]"
"If one eats only sesame seeds and practices in this manner, one will attain purity.
Having taken the sesame, he would either crush it into powder or extract its oil.
Or they may consume various kinds of medicinal preparations for the sake of nourishment. Śāriputra,
I know this matter, and I likewise practice in that same way.
"What was my practice of taking hemp as food?
Śāriputra, I took only a single grain to eat, never adding a second."

Later, at another time, because of eating sesame seeds, my limbs became heavy and stout, or perhaps even glossy; yet I did not form the thought that I should again exceed that measure and take more sesame to eat. I took only a single grain, never adding a second, thinking: "In this way, I shall practice asceticism."
At that time, there were people who came and spoke these words:
"In former days, your appearance was wondrous, excellent, and dignified, and you possessed a majestic radiance; why has it now vanished?"
"Even with such rigorous and arduous cultivation, his physical appearance remains like this! Śāriputra,
although he practices in this way, he cannot attain even a small portion of the supreme dharmas among humans, let alone the most excellent realization of noble knowledge and vision.
To speak at length, up until the exhaustion of the path of birth and death, after which one is no longer reborn.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Among the world there is a class of brahmins who do not eat anything at all, considering this to be purity, and they speak thus:"
"If one does not eat any food whatsoever, practicing in this manner, one attains purity.
Thus spoke Śāriputra.

I knew this matter and likewise practiced accordingly; I did not eat any food whatsoever. Because I did not eat, my body became extremely emaciated; thus it was said at length regarding my practice of asceticism.
Even the crowds of people came and spoke these words: "Alas, alas!
Śramaṇa Gautama!"
Your appearance is emaciated and gaunt like that of a *maṅyū* bird; your former countenance was wondrous, excellent, and dignified, and it also possessed majestic radiance—why has it now vanished?
"Through such rigorous and arduous cultivation, his countenance and physique have become like this!
Śāriputra, at that time, I secretly thought to myself:

"The various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of the world undergo extreme sufferings and further subject their bodies to mutilation and coercion; they do all this for the sake of their own practices, seeking thereby to attain purity."
Within this regard, I have likewise followed their practices; even if my body were ground to dust like its finest particles, there would be no benefit whatsoever.

Thus, throughout the past and future ages, as well as in the present, all śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others have undergone extreme sufferings, further subjecting themselves to mutilation and bodily oppression—all for the sake of their own conduct in pursuit of purity.
In this regard, I followed all those practices; even if my body had been shattered into pieces as fine as dust, there would have been no benefit at all.
I shall no longer subject my body to such bitter and oppressive hardship.
Since he was unable to attain even a small portion of the superior dharmas among human beings, how much less could he realize the most excellent state of noble knowledge and vision?
Therefore, one knows that this path is not the path of perfect enlightenment; I shall no longer practice it.
"Śāriputra! At that time, I further reflected:
'After my initial renunciation, I went to the Jambu tree within the Śākya grove and sat down with composure; the sun's shadow did not shift, and its shade remained cool and protective.'"

At that time, being free from all defilements of desire and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained evaluation, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, I realized the first dhyāna; this is the right path.
Having realized it as it truly is, I have diligently traversed various paths in all places; yet outside of this right path, there is no other path that is true.
Therefore, why should I now, like all these others, take up the path by starving myself until my body is emaciated and further weakened by exhaustion, thereby bringing about its own ruin?
"I should now eat whatever food is available.
While I was thinking this, a certain non-Buddhist practitioner who followed the path of ascetic seers, knowing my thoughts, came to where I was and said to me:
"Venerable Gautama!..."
"You must not retreat from your ascetic practices.
From the pores of my body, I shall emit majestic light to assist you, so that your limbs and members may naturally flourish and be strengthened."
"Śāriputra! At that time, I further thought to myself:
'That I do not eat any food at all has been heard and known by everyone in the kingdoms, cities, and villages. (O Śramaṇa Gautama!)"
Practicing asceticism, he abstained from all food, and his body became emaciated.
In the present age, some say there are ascetic sages who emit majestic light from their bodies to provide assistance and nourishment.
"Would not those various groups of people consider me a liar?
Therefore, fearing such falsehood and detesting the slanderous words of sages and saints, I have desisted and will not accept them."
"Śāriputra! Having had this thought, I gradually increased the amount and consumed whatever was available to sustain my life—whether it was mung bean broth, soybean broth, or red bean broth."
Thus, by gradually consuming food as needed, his physical strength and vital energy were produced step by step.
Once this strength had arisen, he first went to the Dragon River and then to the Nairañjanā River; having arrived, he slowly bathed his body until it was pure and refreshed.
Proceeding by stages, I arrived at a village where there was a woman named Sujātā, who offered me milk-rice.

Having eaten it, I went to the dwelling place of the seer Ṛṣipatana to seek auspicious grass (*śālistamba*). Having obtained it, I took hold of it and proceeded by stages toward the Great Bodhi Tree. Upon arrival, I circumambulated the tree three times to the right; beneath that tree, I spread the auspicious grass all around, inside and out, to serve as my seat.

“Śāriputra! At that time, I sat cross-legged upon it, with body erect and mindfulness established; free from all defilements of desire and unwholesome states, with directed thought and evaluation, born of seclusion, joy and happiness, I realized the first dhyāna.”

Next, one should still the applied and sustained thought; with internal purity, abiding in one-pointedness, free from applied and sustained thought, one realizes the second dhyāna, which is born of concentration and characterized by joy and bliss.

Next, one should dwell in equanimity, free from joy and craving, mindful and clearly comprehending; experiencing a sublime happiness with the body, as the noble ones describe it, one attains the third dhyāna, characterized by equanimity and mindfulness, and the sublime happiness born of freedom from joy.

Next, one should completely sever both suffering and pleasure as before; being entirely detached from whatever arises that is pleasing or distressing to the mind, one attains the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant, characterized by equanimity and pure mindfulness.

"Śāriputra! At that time, I dwelt in a state of meditative equipoise (samāhita-citta) that was pure and stainless, free from the karma of even the mild grades of secondary afflictions, and remained unshakable. During the first watch of the night, I realized, in accordance with reality, the clear vision of the divine eye (divyacakṣus-jñānāloka), and my mind became perfectly awakened."

Śāriputra! That which I have realized is the purified divine eye, which surpasses the human eye; it perceives all sentient beings in the world—their birth and death, their beauty and ugliness, whether they are noble or base—and knows, in accordance with reality, all that they receive as the fruit of their karma.

If there are sentient beings who, through body, speech, and mind, commit unwholesome deeds, revile the noble ones, and give rise to wrong views—due to the accumulation of such karma of wrong views, at the breaking up of the body after death, they fall into the evil destinies and are born in the hells.

If there are sentient beings who, regarding body, speech, and mind, perform various wholesome karmas, do not slander the noble ones, and give rise to right view—due to the accumulation of such karma of right view—when their bodies perish and their lives end, they are reborn in the happy realms among the celestial worlds.
Regarding such matters as these, I perceive and know them all with my purified divine eye.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, at that time, I dwelt successively in a state of samādhi—pure, stainless, free from the karma of minor secondary afflictions, and established in immovability. During the middle watch of the night, I realized, in accordance with reality, the clear knowledge of recollecting past lives, and my mind became well-awakened and lucid.
Śāriputra! The knowledge of past lives that I have realized enables me to know various matters of the past, namely:
one birth, two births, three, four, or five births; ten, twenty, or even a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, and countless hundreds of thousands of births.
Thus, throughout countless lifetimes, regarding the events of the kalpas of formation and destruction— whether in the process of forming or decaying—
he [remembers] his former caste, his former name, and his former lineage.
Such are their physical forms;
such are their food and drink;
such are their lifespans, as well as their experiences of suffering and pleasure.
"This ceases and that arises; that ceases and this arises.
Thus, through my power of knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñānabala*), I recollect such innumerable matters as they truly are.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

At that time, I dwelt successively in a state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita-citta*), pure and stainless, free from the karma of even the mild secondary afflictions, remaining steadfast and unmoving. Then, during the final watch of the night, I realized, as it truly is, the knowledge and vision of the destruction of the outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya-jñāna-vidyā*), and my mind became perfectly awakened and clear.

In due course, when the morning star appeared, the Auspicious One, the Joyful One—the Great Dragon among men, the Lion among men, the Great Sage among men, the Valiant One among men, the Lotus of manifold colors among men, the White Lotus among men, the Supreme among men, the Unsurpassed Tamer among men, the Charioteer of men—came to know what was to be known, to attain what was to be attained, to awaken to what was to be awakened to, and to realize what was to be realized in every respect.
Thus, all these, in a single instant, give rise to the corresponding mind and, through knowledge as it truly is, achieve the path of perfect enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
I know that there are śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas in the world who speak thus:
"If a person is young, with a radiant complexion, glossy hair on the crown of the head, vigorous spirit, and full mental strength;..."
At exactly twenty years of age, or slightly over twenty, such a person is able to practice in accordance with right wisdom.

However, if there is another person whose life has reached old age and senility, whose mental and physical faculties have declined, and who is about to pass away, such a person is unable to practice in accordance with that right wisdom.
"Śāriputra! I am now aged and decrepit, nearly eighty years old, and expect to depart from this life soon.
It is just as when an old, dilapidated cart is kept turning by being bound with various ropes; I am exactly like that!"

"Śāriputra! You should travel extensively, from country to country and from town to town, and observe all those śrāvaka disciples regarding the Tathāgata’s body, his supernormal powers, his supreme wisdom, and his eloquence."
These five things have all diminished. Śāriputra!

If someone were to carry a fire bowl upon their head, traveling from country to country and from town to town, wandering in this manner, it would not be considered difficult; [but this decline is far more so].
If one does not allow superior wisdom and eloquence to diminish, that is indeed difficult. Furthermore, Śāriputra,

suppose there is a person who, although encountering the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, appearing in the world, and who hears him proclaim with a pure mind the correct teachings regarding the nature of suffering, the nature of pleasure, and the nature of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure— yet such a person instead regards these as false and lost teachings.
Śāriputra! One should not regard the Buddha’s correct speech as a deceptive or erroneous teaching. Why is this?

The Tathāgata, the Great Teacher, having appeared in the world, with a pure mind proclaims correct speech regarding phenomena that are painful, pleasant, or neither painful nor pleasant; this is a teaching free from error.

“Śāriputra! Just as four Tathāgatas appeared in the world during this Bhadrakalpa, so too the śrāvaka disciples of these four Buddhas have continued down to the present day with a lifespan of one hundred years; they are all fully endowed with mindfulness, conduct, wisdom, and longevity.”
For example, it is like a strong man who, holding a stiff bow, shoots straight and hits the mark every time. Śāriputra,
the śrāvaka disciples of the three preceding Tathāgatas were also just like this.
They were fully endowed with mindfulness, conduct, wisdom, and longevity; every single one of them was able to approach and inquire about the meaning of the various dharmas day after day. Śāriputra!
Now, within my Dharma, among the śrāvaka disciples, there is not even one who is able to pose a question, let alone one who could do so repeatedly.

Furthermore, having heard what I have spoken once, they are unable to thoroughly understand the meaning and principles of the words and phrases therein; how much less so for the other disciples of the final age?

At times, when eating and drinking, one becomes attached to their flavors; at times, one is overcome by sleep and fatigue; at times, during physical movement, rest, or the acts of defecation and urination—indeed, in all such activities—one is entirely obstructed and hindered.
Śāriputra! The śrāvaka disciples of the three previous Buddhas had lifespans of great duration; that the present lifespan is but one hundred years is exceedingly swift. Śāriputra!
When more than a hundred years have passed, their superior wisdom and eloquence will diminish and decline. Śāriputra!
At that time, the śrāvaka disciples will regard the authentic teachings spoken by the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, as false and lost dharmas.
Śāriputra! One should not, on account of the Buddha’s correct speech, fall into error. Why is this?

When the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, appears in the world, regarding phenomena that are painful, pleasant, or neither painful nor pleasant, he speaks with a pure mind using correct speech; this is a teaching free from error or loss.
At that time, there was a venerable elder in the assembly named Nāgārjuna.
Not far from the Buddha, he stood by the Buddha’s side, holding a peacock-feather fan.
At that moment, he set aside his fan, went before the Buddha, joined his palms in prostration, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Now that I have heard this True Dharma, my body hairs stand on end and I am filled with great joy."
World-Honored One!
What is the name of this sutra? How should we uphold it?
The Buddha said, "Nāgārakṣita!
This True Dharma is now called 'The Rising of the Body Hairs in Joy'."
"You should receive and uphold this title.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the assembly of bhikṣus in the most excellent forest within the most excellent great city of Vaiśālī, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and accepted it with faith.
The Sūtra on the Hair on the Body Standing on End from Joy, Spoken by the Buddha, Volume II.
